Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN) -- Police and soldiers killed at least 133 people during two days of riots between Muslims and Christians in Nigeria last year, Human Rights Watch alleged Monday. Anti-riot policemen patrol the streets in Jos, Nigeria, following riots between Christians and Muslims. Most of the victims of violence by security forces were young Muslim men, often unarmed, the group charged in testimony before a state commission examining the riots and in a separate report. More than 700 people died in the violence last November, the group said, citing local religious authorities on both sides of the divide. A 26-year-old mechanic described seeing anti-riot police known as MOPOLs hunting down people near where he worked. "I saw them enter one house just across the street from us," the unnamed witness said. "We heard shots and later we saw five bodies there. Anyone they found hiding in the garage, they shot them. They combed the garage hunting for people. This went on for about 10 minutes or so. Then they returned to their truck and left." Another witness described police units going from house to house, summarily executing unarmed men and boys. A third said he saw an unarmed shopkeeper plead for his life. Police ordered him to lie down on the ground, the witness said. "He kept saying, 'Please God, allow me to live.'... One of them said, 'Today you go die,' and then he shot him in the side. Then the same MOPOL shot him again. As he was going to shoot him a third time, the other MOPOL said ... 'Leave it, he's already dead.'" The shopkeeper managed to drag himself to a neighbor's house, where the neighbor tried to stop the bleeding from wounds to the back and abdomen. Police then returned and shot tear gas into the neighbor's house, he testified. The shopkeeper "died a short time later," the neighbor said. In the report, released Monday, Human Rights Watch says it "documented 133 of these killings but believes that the actual number of arbitrary killings by security forces may be substantially higher than these figures." James Manook, a spokesman for Plateau State where the violence occurred, said the Human Rights Watch claims are "one of the issues that the commission has under inquiry, and given that - I do not want to comment while it's under investigation." However, he added, " I assure you that we remain respectful of the rule of law." The clashes followed a dispute over an election that pitted a Christian candidate against a Muslim one in late November 2008. Police and soldiers responded to the riots with deadly force, on the same day the governor of the state issued a "shoot-on-sight" order, Human Rights Watch said. The group based its allegations on 151 interviews in the city of Jos in Nigeria's Plateau State, it says in the report. It withheld the names of many of the people it interviewed over the course of 18 days in December 2008 and February 2009. The report includes photographs of burned-out mosques, Christian boarding schools, and homes and businesses. The rights group said the state commission examining the riots should investigate and call for the prosecution of security forces involved. "At least 130 men were killed by members of the very institutions charged with protecting them," said Corinne Dufka, senior West Africa researcher at Human Rights Watch. "These investigative bodies owe it to the victims and their families to conduct a thorough and impartial investigation into these extremely serious allegations." Eric Guttschuss, a Human Rights Watch researcher, testified before the commission Monday. There is a history of religious violence in central Nigeria, where majority-Muslim north Africa meets largely Christian sub-Saharan Africa. Human Rights Watch estimates that more than 1,000 people were killed in riots in 2001. Local religious leaders in Jos have been trying to bridge the differences, including setting up a soccer league with teams on which Christians and Muslims play side-by-side. CNN's Christian Purefoy contributed to this report.

LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN) — Human Rights Watch said Monday that Nigerian police officers and soldiers killed no fewer than 133 people during two days of Muslim-Christian rioting the previous year.

In Jos, Nigeria, anti-riot police were seen patrolling after the clashes between Christians and Muslims. According to the rights organization, most of those killed by security personnel were young Muslim men, many of whom were not armed. The allegations were presented both in testimony to a state commission investigating the unrest and in a separate report.

Human Rights Watch said more than 700 people were killed in the November violence, citing figures from local religious leaders from both communities.

One 26-year-old mechanic said he watched anti-riot police officers, known as MOPOLs, search for people near his workplace. The witness, whose name was not disclosed, said the officers entered a house across the street. He reported hearing gunfire and later seeing five bodies there. He said anyone discovered hiding in the garage was shot, and that officers searched the garage for about 10 minutes before returning to their truck and leaving.

A second witness said police units moved from one home to another, carrying out immediate executions of unarmed men and boys.

A third witness said he saw an unarmed shopkeeper beg not to be killed. According to that witness, police told the man to lie on the ground. The shopkeeper repeatedly prayed to be spared, but one officer reportedly told him he would die that day and then shot him in the side. The same MOPOL officer shot him again. As he prepared to fire a third time, another MOPOL officer told him to stop, saying the man was already dead.

The wounded shopkeeper was still able to drag himself to a neighbor’s home, where the neighbor attempted to control bleeding from injuries to his back and abdomen. The neighbor testified that police later came back and fired tear gas into the house. The shopkeeper died soon afterward, the neighbor said.

In its report, issued Monday, Human Rights Watch stated that it had documented 133 such killings, but believed the real number of unlawful killings by security forces could be far greater.

James Manook, a spokesman for Plateau State, where the unrest took place, said the accusations raised by Human Rights Watch were among the matters being reviewed by the commission. Because the issue was under investigation, he said, he did not want to comment further. He added, however, that the state remained committed to respecting the rule of law.

The violence erupted after a disagreement over an election in late November 2008 involving a Christian candidate and a Muslim candidate. Human Rights Watch said police and soldiers used lethal force against rioters on the same day the state governor issued an order to “shoot on sight.”

The group said its conclusions were based on 151 interviews conducted in Jos, located in Nigeria’s Plateau State. Human Rights Watch said it withheld many interviewees’ names. The interviews were carried out over 18 days in December 2008 and February 2009.

The report also contained photographs showing burned mosques, Christian boarding schools, houses, and businesses.

Human Rights Watch urged the state commission looking into the riots to investigate the conduct of security forces and recommend prosecutions where appropriate.

“At least 130 men were killed by members of the very institutions charged with protecting them,” said Corinne Dufka, Human Rights Watch’s senior West Africa researcher. She said the investigative bodies had a duty to victims and their relatives to carry out a complete and unbiased inquiry into the grave allegations.

Eric Guttschuss, a researcher with Human Rights Watch, gave testimony before the commission on Monday.

Central Nigeria has a long record of religious conflict, lying near the point where the largely Muslim north of Africa meets the mostly Christian sub-Saharan region. Human Rights Watch estimates that riots in 2001 left more than 1,000 people dead.

In Jos, local religious leaders have attempted to reduce tensions, including by creating a soccer league with teams made up of both Christian and Muslim players.

CNN’s Christian Purefoy contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.output:
**Human Rights Watch alleges Nigerian security forces killed 133 during Jos riots**

**LAGOS, Nigeria** — Nigerian police and soldiers killed at least 133 people during deadly sectarian unrest in the central city of Jos in 2008, Human Rights Watch alleged in a report, calling for an independent investigation and prosecutions of those responsible.

The violence erupted in November 2008 after a disputed local government election in Jos, the capital of Plateau State, where tensions between Muslim and Christian communities have repeatedly turned deadly. Hundreds of people were killed as mobs attacked homes, places of worship and businesses.

But Human Rights Watch said many of the deaths were not caused by rioters. The group alleged that Nigerian security forces carried out arbitrary killings after being deployed to restore order, targeting residents in several neighborhoods.

“Soldiers and police were meant to protect civilians, not execute them,” the rights group said, urging Nigerian authorities to identify officers involved and hold them accountable.

Witnesses interviewed by Human Rights Watch described security personnel shooting people at close range, dragging men from homes and killing detainees, the organization said. The group said many of the victims were young Muslim men, though the broader violence involved attacks by both Muslim and Christian mobs.

Nigerian authorities have previously said security forces were sent in to stop the unrest and prevent further bloodshed. Officials have often blamed the violence in Jos on political manipulation, religious extremism and long-running disputes over land, citizenship rights and political control.

Jos sits in Nigeria’s Middle Belt, a region where the country’s largely Muslim north meets its predominantly Christian south. Competition over jobs, land and political representation has fueled recurring clashes, often framed along religious and ethnic lines.

Human Rights Watch said the 2008 killings fit a wider pattern of impunity in Nigeria, where security forces have frequently been accused of excessive force but rarely face prosecution.

The organization called on the Nigerian government to conduct a transparent inquiry into the alleged killings, compensate victims’ families and reform security operations during civil unrest.

The Jos riots remain one of several major outbreaks of communal violence in Plateau State, where cycles of revenge attacks have continued to claim lives in the years since.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate the full text of a breaking news report from Lagos on allegations of security-force abuses in Plateau State, Nigeria, including witness testimony, HRW findings, and official response.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS REPORT**

**LAGOS, Nigeria —** Allegations of serious abuses by Nigerian security forces in Plateau State have intensified following witness accounts and findings released by Human Rights Watch, which accuse troops and other security personnel of unlawful killings, arbitrary arrests, and the destruction of property during operations in communities affected by recurring violence.

Residents from several communities in Plateau, a north-central state long troubled by clashes involving farming and herding groups, armed attacks, and reprisals, told reporters that security forces deployed to restore order instead carried out raids that left civilians dead and homes damaged.

“I saw them enter the compound shouting and firing,” said one witness, a resident who asked to be identified only as *Musa* for fear of retaliation. “They said they were looking for attackers, but they beat people who were not armed. My brother was taken away, and for days we did not know where he was.”

Another resident, *Grace*, said her family fled after security personnel allegedly set parts of her neighborhood ablaze during a search operation. “We were already afraid because of the attacks in nearby villages,” she said. “Then the people who were supposed to protect us came, and everything became worse.”

Human Rights Watch said its researchers interviewed victims, relatives, community leaders, and local activists, and reviewed photographs, video footage, and medical accounts consistent with allegations of abuse. The rights group said the testimony pointed to a pattern of excessive force and collective punishment during security operations in Plateau State.

According to HRW, witnesses described security personnel beating detainees, firing at civilians, and arresting men and boys without warrants. The organization said some families were denied information about the whereabouts of detained relatives, raising concerns about enforced disappearance and incommunicado detention.

“Authorities must ensure that security operations protect civilians rather than deepen the cycle of violence,” HRW said in its findings. “Allegations of unlawful killings, arbitrary detention, and destruction of property should be investigated promptly, independently, and transparently.”

The group also called on the Nigerian government to provide reparations to victims, prosecute security personnel implicated in abuses, and ensure that all detainees are either charged with recognizable offenses or released.

Plateau State has seen repeated outbreaks of deadly violence, often attributed to disputes over land, grazing routes, ethnicity, religion, and political representation. Local communities have frequently accused authorities of failing to prevent attacks or of responding too slowly when violence erupts.

Nigeria’s military and police have previously rejected allegations of systematic abuse, saying security forces operate under strict rules of engagement and are deployed to protect civilians from armed groups.

In response to the latest allegations, a government security spokesperson said authorities would examine any credible claims but denied that troops were targeting civilians.

“The Nigerian security forces are in Plateau State to restore peace and protect law-abiding citizens,” the spokesperson said. “Any personnel found to have acted outside the law will face appropriate disciplinary measures. However, we caution against unverified reports that may inflame tensions or undermine ongoing security operations.”

The Plateau State government also urged residents to cooperate with security agencies and avoid spreading rumors, while promising to support investigations into specific complaints.

Civil society groups say accountability is essential to rebuilding trust between communities and the state.

“When people fear both attackers and the security forces sent to protect them, the situation becomes extremely dangerous,” said a Lagos-based human rights lawyer. “The government needs to show that no one is above the law.”

Families of alleged victims say they want answers.

“We are not asking for revenge,” said Grace. “We want the truth. We want to know who gave the orders and why innocent people were treated like criminals.”

Human Rights Watch said it would continue monitoring developments in Plateau State and urged Nigerian authorities to allow independent investigators, journalists, and humanitarian workers safe access to affected areas.

The allegations come as Nigeria faces mounting security challenges across several regions, including insurgency in the northeast, banditry in the northwest, separatist tensions in the southeast, and farmer-herder violence in the Middle Belt.

For now, residents in parts of Plateau State say fear remains high.

“At night, nobody sleeps well,” Musa said. “We do not know if the next sound will be attackers, soldiers, or someone coming to take another person away.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Human Rights Watch Says Nigerian Forces Carried Out Arbitrary Killings After Jos Election Violence**

**LAGOS, Nigeria —** Nigerian police and soldiers arbitrarily killed scores of people while responding to deadly sectarian and political violence that followed disputed local elections in the central city of Jos in November 2008, Human Rights Watch said in a report released Tuesday.

The New York-based rights group said security forces killed at least 133 people, most of them Muslim men, during and after clashes that erupted in Jos, the capital of Plateau state, after the November 27 local government elections. The violence pitted supporters of rival political parties and members of Christian and Muslim communities against one another in one of Nigeria’s most volatile “Middle Belt” cities.

Human Rights Watch said its findings were based on interviews with witnesses, survivors, community leaders, religious officials, journalists, medical workers and government officials. The group said many of the killings attributed to security forces did not occur in exchanges of fire or during active efforts to stop rioting, but instead appeared to be summary executions.

“Security forces were deployed to restore order, but some police and soldiers became perpetrators of unlawful killings,” the organization said. It called on Nigerian authorities to investigate the alleged abuses and prosecute officers responsible.

The Jos violence began after supporters of the opposition All Nigeria Peoples Party challenged results in the Jos North local government election, which the ruling People’s Democratic Party was reported to have won. Tensions quickly spread through mixed neighborhoods, with mobs attacking residents based on their perceived religion or ethnicity, burning homes, shops, mosques and churches.

Jos lies along Nigeria’s religious and ethnic fault line, between the mainly Muslim north and largely Christian south. Political competition in the city often overlaps with disputes between so-called “indigenes” — groups considered native to Plateau state, many of them Christian — and “settlers,” a term often applied to Hausa-Fulani Muslims, even those whose families have lived in the area for generations. Access to jobs, scholarships, political office and land is frequently shaped by those classifications, fueling resentment.

Human Rights Watch said hundreds of civilians were killed by mobs during the unrest, but its report focused on killings allegedly carried out by government security forces after police and military units were sent into the city. Witnesses told the group that soldiers and police shot unarmed men in the street, pulled men from homes and executed detainees in several neighborhoods.

In one area, the group said, witnesses described security personnel separating men from women and children before shooting the men. In other cases, bodies reportedly showed signs of close-range gunfire. Human Rights Watch said some victims were killed after the main street fighting had subsided.

The organization said the pattern of killings suggested that some members of the security forces targeted residents based on their religion or ethnicity, particularly in predominantly Muslim neighborhoods. It said the government’s failure to hold security personnel accountable in past incidents of communal violence had contributed to a climate of impunity.

Nigerian officials have previously said security forces were deployed to prevent wider bloodshed and restore public order after the Jos clashes overwhelmed local police. Authorities at the time imposed a curfew and sent soldiers into affected neighborhoods. The federal and state governments also announced inquiries into the violence.

Human Rights Watch said those steps were not sufficient unless they led to credible prosecutions.

“The Nigerian government has repeatedly set up commissions of inquiry after outbreaks of violence, but their findings are often ignored and those responsible are rarely punished,” the group said. “Victims and their families are entitled to justice, and the security forces must be subject to the rule of law.”

The organization urged President Umaru Yar’Adua’s government to ensure an independent investigation into the conduct of police and military personnel in Jos, suspend officers credibly implicated in abuses, and make the results public. It also called for compensation for victims’ families and reforms to prevent the use of excessive force during civil unrest.

The Jos killings were among several episodes in which Nigerian security forces have been accused by rights groups of using lethal force unlawfully, including in responses to communal clashes, protests and insurgent attacks. Nigerian police and military authorities have often denied systematic abuses, saying officers operate under difficult and dangerous conditions.

Plateau state has seen repeated bouts of deadly violence since 2001, with thousands killed in clashes linked to political power, land disputes, religion and ethnic identity. Rights groups say the lack of accountability after each crisis has deepened mistrust among communities and made further violence more likely.

Human Rights Watch said the November 2008 unrest underscored the urgent need for Nigerian authorities to address both immediate security-force abuses and the underlying discrimination and political exclusion that have helped drive conflict in Jos.

“The government cannot restore lasting peace in Jos simply by sending in troops,” the group said. “It must also ensure that those troops do not kill civilians with impunity.”

The violence erupted in [LOCATION/STATE] after tensions between religious groups escalated into clashes, with homes, shops and places of worship attacked, according to witnesses and local officials. CNN has not independently verified all of the allegations in the report. Nigeria’s [police/military/government spokesperson] did not immediately respond to a request for comment. **Nigeria orders troops to shoot on sight after deadly Jos riots**

**JOS, Nigeria —** Nigerian authorities imposed a shoot-on-sight order in the central city of Jos after days of Muslim-Christian violence left scores of people dead, homes and mosques burned, and thousands forced to flee.

The clashes, which erupted in and around Jos, the capital of Plateau State, were among the worst in a long-running cycle of sectarian and ethnic violence in Nigeria’s “Middle Belt,” where the mostly Muslim north meets the largely Christian south. Residents described gangs armed with machetes, knives and firearms attacking neighborhoods, setting buildings ablaze and blocking roads.

Officials placed the city under a round-the-clock curfew and deployed soldiers to restore order. State authorities said troops had been instructed to fire on anyone violating the curfew or caught attacking others, a measure they said was necessary to stop the bloodshed.

Casualty figures remained disputed. Government officials initially gave lower tolls, while local religious and community leaders reported far higher numbers. Human rights groups said the deaths likely ran into the hundreds, with victims from both Muslim and Christian communities. Hospitals and aid workers struggled to count bodies as violence spread to surrounding villages.

Human Rights Watch called on Nigerian authorities to investigate the killings and prosecute those responsible, including members of security forces if they used unlawful force. The group said Nigeria’s failure to punish perpetrators of earlier violence in Jos had helped fuel repeated revenge attacks.

“Unless those responsible for organizing and carrying out these killings are brought to justice, the cycle of violence will continue,” the organization said.

Jos has seen repeated outbreaks of violence linked to religious identity, political power, land disputes and competition between communities classified as “indigenes” and those regarded as “settlers.” Though often described as Muslim-Christian clashes, analysts say the conflict is also rooted in local grievances over jobs, elections and access to government benefits.

Relief agencies said displaced families were sheltering in churches, mosques, army barracks and police stations. Many residents said they feared returning home despite the military presence, warning that the calm remained fragile.

Nigeria’s federal government urged restraint and promised an inquiry, but rights advocates said previous commissions had produced little accountability. They warned that without prosecutions and reforms to address the underlying disputes, Jos could again descend into violence.
